Yet the opponent must still assert they connect (to explain burning). How can things that preclude each other's stable existence also be connected?","madhyamaka":"Mutual preclusion: fire destroys fuel, fuel's stable presence implies no fire. They can't stably co-exist. Yet burning requires their connection. The opponent faces a dilemma within a dilemma: they're different (v.5's problem), they need fitness (v.6's problem), AND they preclude each other (v.7's problem).","quantum":"Particle-antiparticle pairs preclude each other — they annihilate on contact. Yet they must \"meet\" for annihilation to occur. The interaction that connects them is the same interaction that destroys them. Similarly, fire's connection to fuel IS the destruction of fuel.","bridge":"Both annihilation and burning involve entities whose very interaction is mutually destructive. Connection = destruction. This creates a paradox for inherent difference: the connection that should unite them is the very thing that eliminates one of them.","accessible":"A match and water: they \"preclude\" each other (water extinguishes the match). Yet they must meet for the extinguishing to happen. The connection between them is their mutual exclusion. Paradoxical if they're supposed to be stably connected.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, fire and fuel interact through mutual transformation — fuel becomes heat, fire depends on fuel. The paradox arises only when we try to make this interaction work between INHERENTLY different, independent entities.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying fire and fuel can't interact. Showing that INHERENTLY different things that PRECLUDE each other face a paradox: the very connection they need destroys the basis for that connection."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Particle-Antiparticle Annihilation","score":72,"strength":"High","explanation":"Matter-antimatter pairs are distinct but annihilate on contact — their connection IS their mutual destruction.
